# Capstone

::: {.callout-question}

Can you defend every placement in your system with a number?

:::

The robot is whole now. It tracks a face before she finishes turning, perceives
at the knee instead of the peak, reads meaning where the budget allows and asks
the cloud only when it must, decides when a situation is worth thinking hard
about, moves under a safety envelope, remembers what it was taught and forgets on
request, improves from the little it keeps, and ships into a home with its failure
path and its data boundary both measured. Each of those was a placement, and each
was defended by the one property that bound it.

The capstone asks you to put them together and defend the whole. Not to prove the
robot is smart, but to prove you can say, with numbers, why every part of it lives
where it lives.

## What the capstone asks

The deliverable is the discipline, demonstrated. Present a complete physical AI
system, or a defended partial one, with four things:

A working loop. The robot closes at least one full loop, sensing through acting,
even if some capabilities are stubbed or run at a fallback rung.

A filled placement map. Every capability placed by loop and by box, the way
[the placement chapter](07-placement-and-systems.qmd) built it, with the cost of
each placement measured rather than assumed: latency, energy, and the bytes that
leave the device.

The binding constraint for each. For every placement, the one property that
decided it, named, with the number that forced your hand.

One re-placement. Move a single capability and report the system effect: what
budget it freed, what it cost elsewhere, and whether the whole system got better.

## The bar

The exam is not "did it work." A build that fell short but was measured and
explained demonstrates the discipline; a build that worked but cannot say why does
not. So the defense is the assessment. Name the properties in tension, show the
placement, show the number that bound it, and account for what the choice cost. A
well-instrumented failure, defended, passes. An undefended success is just a demo.

This is the same standard the book applied to itself. Every claim was meant to be
measured, cited, or reasoned, never asserted. The capstone asks you to hold your
own system to it.

## The discipline, in your hands

Physical AI is not machine learning with a motor attached. It is a system coupled
to the world in a closed loop, acting into the same world its next input comes
from, under the limits of a body, in a space that belongs to a person. That
coupling is what makes it a field of its own: it is the regime where the
assumptions its neighbors rely on, that the data is given, that the plant is
known, that the task is bounded, all fail at once. The recurring skill the field
asks for is placement, and the recurring proof is a number.

So here is the test that outlasts the kit. Put a new physical AI problem in front
of yourself, any one, and you should now reach for the same moves without being
told: name the properties in tension, find the one that binds, place the
capability in a loop and a box, defend the choice with a measurement, and watch
what it costs the rest of the system. That habit, not any particular robot, is
what you built. It is the discipline, and it is yours now.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Open question**: one capstone, or a small menu, a companion, a helper, a
  show-and-tell toy, so learners pick the embodiment they care about? The
  deliverable and the bar are the same whichever they choose.
- **Watch**: assess the defense, not the demo. The temptation is to reward the
  robot that worked; reward the student who can say why every placement is where
  it is, and what it cost.

:::
